newsitem.title: USA: Miami oversight board says no deadline extension.
newsitem.headline: Miami oversight board says no deadline extension.

text.p: A Florida state-appointed oversight board on Tuesday refused to extend a deadline for the financially strapped city of Miami to submit its recovery plan.
The decision meant the city still faced an April 15 deadline to submit a balanced five-year budget to the board. The Miami City Commission had asked for a 45-day extension.
The board has a month after the deadline to review the plan and seek revisions.

In a conference call at an emergency meeting convened late Tuesday, members of the Miami Financial Oversight Board unanimously denied the request by the Miami City Commission to extend the deadline, saying that the difficult decisions to be made by the city cannot wait.
Miami City Manager Ed Marquez told board members that a draft budget was prepared and had been submitted to city commissioners for their modification and approval.
When queried by board members about the budget plan, Marquez said he would not recommend substantive changes to the plan submitted Tuesday to city commissioners.

"I think it's imperative that we proceed without any further delay," board member Robert Beatty said. "I think 45 days is unreasonable, given that Ed has prepared a first draft of a plan and he is prepared to move that plan forward."
Beatty's motion denying the request was approved on a voice vote and meeting adjourned within 10 minutes.

Lt. Gov. Buddy MacKay, appointed by Florida Gov. Lawton Chiles to head the commission, asked staff to go ahead and see what legal options the state would have if Miami officials were unable or unwilling to make the difficult financial decisions needed to keep the city from going broke.
"I hope that doesn't happen, and I'm not trying to suggest that we are not willing to cooperate," MacKay said. "But I do think we ought to be ready to understand what we do next."
Marquez said Monday the final outside audit of city finances was expected on May 5. The audit was expected to confirm that the city's cumulative deficit was $68 million at the beginning of 1997.
The board has approved a 1997 budget that closed the gap, largely through land sales and other one-time revenues.
